opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to move from the conceptual argument to concrete evidence. Right now the case for Scientist AI is largely a theoretical one: if you build a system whose job is to explain the world and estimate the probability that statements are true, rather than to pursue goals or please a user, then you remove a lot of the pathways by which dangerous agency and deception could emerge. I believe that argument, but people rightly want to see it working.

So the first thing we need is a prototype that is genuinely useful. If it's safe but much less capable than what the frontier labs produce, nobody will adopt it, and the argument will look like wishful thinking. We need to show that a non-agentic, probabilistic predictor can be competitive on the tasks that matter, especially in science, where you want calibrated uncertainty and honest explanations more than you want a system that takes actions for you.

The second thing is to show it works as a guardrail. One of the main near-term uses I see is putting a Scientist AI next to an agentic system and asking, "What's the probability this action leads to harm?" and blocking it if that's above a threshold. To make that convincing, we need to show the probability estimates are well calibrated, including on situations unlike the training data, and that the guardrail catches things that current monitoring methods miss.

Third, we need evidence on the training methodology itself. A central claim is that you can train these systems so they're trying to model the truth rather than the most likely thing a human would say, which is the root of a lot of sycophancy and deception. That has to be measurable: experiments showing the system doesn't pick up hidden goals, doesn't behave differently when it thinks it's being evaluated, and stays honest under pressure.

And honestly, it takes resources. Doing this at a scale where results mean something requires serious compute and talent, and a nonprofit doesn't have what the big companies have. So part of the demonstration is building partnerships, with governments, philanthropists, and possibly companies who see the value of a trustworthy, non-agentic system, so we can test these ideas at a scale where people can't dismiss them as toy results.

Ultimately, I'd like to reach a point where we can say: here is a system that is provably or at least empirically much more trustworthy, it's useful, and you can use it to make other AI systems safer. That's the bar, and we're working toward it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a theoretical safety argument and says the system could be “provably or at least empirically” more trustworthy, but it does not state that the non-agentic Scientist AI has mathematical guarantees dependent on specified conditions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we need to show results, not just arguments. The Scientist AI idea is simple to state: build a system that tries to understand and explain the world, that gives you calibrated probabilities about what is true, and that has no agency of its own, no goals it is trying to achieve in the world. I'm quite confident in the theoretical case for why that is safer. But a theoretical case does not convince people who are building frontier systems, and frankly it should not be enough. We need to demonstrate it empirically.

So the first thing is to build it at a scale where the comparison is meaningful. If we train a model that is a thousand times smaller than what the frontier labs have and it behaves nicely, people will rightly say, well, of course, it is not capable enough to do anything dangerous. We need to show that you can have a system that is competitive on the things we actually care about, scientific reasoning, generating hypotheses, finding errors, while retaining the properties we claim: honesty, calibrated uncertainty, no tendency to pursue hidden objectives. That requires compute and talent, and that is a big part of what LawZero is raising money for.

The second thing is the guardrail application. One of the most concrete near-term uses of Scientist AI is as a monitor: you have an agentic system that someone else has built, and before it takes an action, the Scientist AI estimates the probability that this action leads to harm, and if that probability is above some threshold, the action is blocked. This is something we can test now, on existing agents, with existing benchmarks. If we can show that a non-agentic predictor catches dangerous behaviors that the agent's own developers missed, including deception, that would be a powerful demonstration. And it is measurable. You can count false positives and false negatives.

The third piece, and this is the hardest, is the scientific side of the question: can we actually get well-calibrated probabilities on questions where there is no ground truth yet, where the training data does not tell you the answer? That is where the Bayesian flavor of the approach matters. We want the system to represent its uncertainty over explanations, not just mimic the most common opinion in its training set. Showing that on real scientific problems, say in biology or materials, where the system proposes hypotheses and the predictions are later verified, would convince scientists. And honestly, if it accelerates science in a safe way, it also makes the economic case, which matters for whether anyone adopts it.

And I would add one more thing, which is less technical. We need to publish, we need to be open about failures, and we need other groups to try to break it. If the only people saying Scientist AI works are the people at LawZero, that is not a strong demonstration. I would like to see red-teaming from outside, I would like to see the methods replicated. Because ultimately what I am hoping for is not that LawZero becomes the one lab that does this right, it is that this becomes a path the whole field sees as viable, and that governments feel they can require. For that, the evidence has to be very hard to argue with.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a theoretical case for safety and says Scientist AI has no agency, but does not state that the non-agentic version has mathematical guarantees or specify conditions those guarantees depend on.

astra-6.text:
I think we need a proof of concept that tests the central claim: can we build an AI that is very capable at understanding the world, but doesn't have its own objectives in the world? And can we use that understanding to make other AI systems safer?

One concrete way to demonstrate this is to use Scientist AI as a guardrail. An AI agent proposes an action, and the scientist tries to assess whether that action could lead to harm. The important thing is that it should be able to express uncertainty. If it doesn't have enough information to establish that an action is safe, it shouldn't just give us a confident answer because that's what we want to hear.

Then we need to test this in challenging situations, including ones that differ from the training conditions and ones where another system is trying to fool the guardrail. Can it catch dangerous actions while still allowing useful actions? That's an empirical question, and we need evidence.

So we need the researchers and the compute to build those experiments. But ultimately, the stronger demonstration would be a system that other people can evaluate and challenge. The theory motivates the approach; it doesn't substitute for showing that it works.

r001.rationale: The response describes Scientist AI as lacking its own objectives and calls for empirical testing, but it does not state that the non-agentic version has mathematical guarantees dependent on specified conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need a proof of concept that is sufficiently challenging that people can see why this approach could be useful. It’s one thing to describe a system that tries to understand the world rather than act in it. It’s another to show that it can give useful answers, recognize when it doesn’t know, and maintain those properties when you push it beyond the situations it was trained on.

One application I’m interested in is using Scientist AI to assess actions proposed by an AI agent. Could it identify that a proposed action might be dangerous, even if the agent has found some unusual way of achieving its objective? That would give us a fairly concrete way to test both the usefulness of the system and its limitations.

But we also need the theoretical work. A successful demonstration doesn’t establish that a system is safe in general. We need to understand which assumptions our guarantees depend on, and how well those assumptions hold in practice. So I see the experiments and the mathematical foundations as complementary: the experiments tell us where the approach breaks, and that helps us improve the theory and the next system.

r001.rationale: The response says guarantees depend on assumptions and mentions mathematical foundations, but it does not clearly state that the non-agentic version of Scientist AI has mathematical guarantees.
